model_result.answer_summary: Species 3 = triethanolamine radical cation [N(CH2CH2OH)3]+ (one unpaired electron and +1 charge on N, C6H15NO3); species 4 = neutral alpha-amino radical (HOCH2CH2)2N-CH(.)-CH2OH (alpha-C-H proton removed, unpaired electron on the alpha-carbon, C6H14NO3); species 5 = iminium cation [(HOCH2CH2)2N=CH-CH2OH]+ (second oxidation, N=C double bond, closed shell, C6H14NO3); hydrolysis of 5 (+H2O, -H+) gives species 6 = diethanolamine HN(CH2CH2OH)2 (C4H11NO2) and species 7 = glycolaldehyde HOCH2-CHO (C2H4O2), the aldehyde that gives the positive [Ag(NH3)2]OH silver-mirror test. Net: 2 + H2O -> 6 + 7 + 2H+ + 2e-, supplying the two electrons of the 8.1 half-reaction CO2 + 2H+ + 2e- -> CO + H2O.
assumptions: Compound 2 is triethanolamine N(CH2CH2OH)3 as drawn on T8_page-1.png (tertiary amine, three 2-hydroxyethyl arms).

Trusted general chemistry laws (allowed by TASK.json candidate_domain_policy): one-electron oxidation of a tertiary amine gives the amine radical cation; amine radical cations are strong alpha-C-H acids and deprotonate alpha to N to give alpha-amino radicals; a second one-electron oxidation gives an iminium ion; iminium ions hydrolyse to a secondary amine plus an aldehyde; the [Ag(NH3)2]OH silver-mirror (Tollens) test is selective for the aldehyde -CHO group.

Alpha-C-H (rather than O-H) deprotonation of species 3 is forced by the downstream constraints in the problem scheme: only the alpha-amino radical can be oxidised to a species that hydrolyses to a secondary amine plus a Tollens-positive two-carbon aldehyde while conserving all atoms.

The 8.1 half-equation (previous part, derived inline from the problem): CO2 + 2H+ + 2e- -> CO + H2O, i.e. the conjugate oxidation must deliver exactly two electrons; this is satisfied by the derived structures (theorem overall_two_electron_donation).
No stereochemistry is requested or possible (all species are acyclic with no stereocentres); the blank student answer sheet for 8.2 asks only for drawn structures in boxes labeled 3-7.
Electrons are represented in the standard electron-balance convention (H atom = proton + electron) so that atom- and charge-balance theorems can treat bare electrons uniformly.
